text: Every AI workload on Azure eventually asks the same question: what hardware actually runs this model? CPU, GPU, or a managed service that picks for you.

CPU handles lightweight inference fine — small embedding models, low-throughput APIs, classical ML scoring that never needed a GPU in the first place. GPU earns its cost for training and heavy inference — fine-tuning an LLM, generating embeddings at high throughput, running image or video models where a CPU would simply be too slow. Managed services like Azure OpenAI's pay-as-you-go and provisioned throughput units abstract the hardware away entirely — you just pay for tokens or reserved capacity.

When you do need to pick compute yourself, Azure's GPU VMs are named by workload, not just GPU count. NC-series covers general AI and ML training and inference — the default starting point. ND-series is built for large-scale deep learning with multiple GPUs per VM. NV-series is tuned for visualization and virtual desktops, not training — an easy mistake to make by VM name alone.

Before committing a compute budget to a size, check what a region actually has available — GPU capacity is scarcer than regular compute. az vm list-skus with a location and a size prefix like Standard_NC lists every matching GPU size actually sellable in that region right now, before you design around a SKU that turns out to be unavailable.
CPU for light work, GPU for heavy work, managed when you'd rather not choose at all. Next up: where the data behind these models — and the embeddings they produce — actually live.
